bp: A blockchain needs a public rule for deciding which transactions get processed and what users pay. That rule is a fee auction: users attach payments, and the miner or block producer chooses what enters the block. The difficulty is that the miner is also a strategic actor. A user and the miner can make a private side agreement outside the public rule, such as promising inclusion while shifting money through a hidden payment. Transaction fee mechanisms study how to design the public rule so these private bargains do not make the intended auction meaningless. This paper asks how much collusion resistance must be checked. Earlier work defined c-Side-Contract-Proofness, meaning safety against a miner secretly coordinating with c users. The paper's main message is stark: once collusion with two users is deterred, larger miner-user coalitions add no new class of threat, assuming ties are broken consistently.
wh: The hard part is that a blockchain fee rule is not only sorting bids. It is sorting bids while the sorter can secretly bargain with the bidders. In an ordinary auction, the seller and bidders are often treated as separate roles with limited outside coordination. In a blockchain, the miner who implements the allocation can cooperate with users who want cheaper or favored inclusion. A designer therefore has to reason about hidden agreements, not just public bids. The size of the coalition seems as if it should matter: a miner plus one user, a miner plus two users, and a miner plus many users might appear to create different attack surfaces. Prior work had already shown a real gap between the one-user and two-user cases. That makes the next question subtle. If two is stronger than one, perhaps three or ten is stronger again. The paper proves that, beyond two, this apparent ladder collapses under consistent tie-breaking.
naive: A smart beginner would try to certify a fee mechanism separately for every possible coalition size. First check whether one user and the miner can profit, then check two users and the miner, then three, and so on. This sounds careful, but it creates an endless design burden because blockchains may have many users in a block. It also hides the main structure of the problem. The question is not whether a larger crowd has more names in it, but whether adding more users creates a fundamentally new way to change bids, payments, or allocation. According to this paper, after the two-user case, larger coalitions do not define a new mechanism class, provided tie cases are handled in a consistent way.
ap: The core idea is to turn a large-collusion question into a small-collusion question. The paper studies classes of transaction fee mechanisms: one class contains mechanisms safe against the miner plus two users, and another contains mechanisms safe against the miner plus any c users for c at least two. It proves these classes are the same, under a relatively minor assumption that ties are broken consistently. In concrete terms, if a mechanism can be exploited by a miner coordinating with a larger group of users, then that exploit is not truly dependent on the whole group. The weakness can already be witnessed by a miner and two users. That means the designer can focus on deterring the smallest coalition that captures the post-one-user difficulty. The title's claim is therefore not a heuristic; it is a classification result about which fee rules survive which collusion tests.
mech: The mechanism being analyzed takes transaction bids and turns them into outcomes: which transactions are included, what each included user pays, and what revenue or utility the miner receives. A side contract lets the miner and a chosen set of users compare the public outcome with a coordinated alternative. In the alternative, some bids, inclusions, or transfers may change so that every member of the coalition is at least as well off and some member is better off. A mechanism is c-Side-Contract-Proof when no such profitable private rearrangement exists for the miner plus c users. The paper's proof compares these safety tests across coalition sizes. First, the one-user case remains special because earlier work shows it does not match the two-user case. Second, for every coalition size c at least two, the paper shows equivalence with the two-user test. The consistent tie-breaking assumption matters because when two public outcomes are otherwise equal, the rule must choose among them in a stable way; otherwise artificial differences in tie choices could create or remove an apparent collusion opportunity. The output of the analysis is not a new fee rule, but a reduction in what must be proven about any fee rule: test resistance to the miner plus two users, and that covers all larger user coalitions in this formal setting.
math: The main mathematical idea is mechanism design, which means choosing rules for self-interested people so that their best available moves do not damage the system's goal. Here the rule maps bids to transaction inclusion and fees. The safety property is a no-profitable-deviation condition: compare the official outcome with every private bargain available to a miner-user coalition, and require that the coalition cannot make itself better off by leaving the rule's intended path. The parameter c is a way of counting coalition size. It turns the vague phrase 'resistant to collusion' into a family of exact tests: safe against one user, safe against two users, safe against c users. The proof result is a set equality: the set of mechanisms passing the two-user test equals the set passing every c-user test for c at least two. Set equality matters because it says two descriptions pick out the same objects. The consistent tie-breaking condition controls boundary cases where values are equal. Without a stable rule for equal outcomes, the mathematics could confuse a harmless tie-choice artifact with a genuine side-contract gain. The tradeoff is precision versus practicality: a formal condition narrows the messy world of private deals into cases that can be checked and compared.
dots: This paper connects blockchain mechanism design to several recurring conference ideas. It is a ranking and auction paper because a scarce block space must be allocated among competing transactions, and the rule must say whose bid earns priority. It is also a security paper because the attacker is not breaking cryptography; the attacker is exploiting incentives around who controls ordering and fees. It neighbors fraud and anomaly work on collusive groups, such as set-level spam detection in the repo's current data, because both ask when a group can create an outcome that individuals could not safely create alone. It also sits near the mempool-auditing blockchain paper in the current data: both concern miners whose transaction choices may be unfair or manipulative. The difference is that mempool auditing studies detection in deployed networks, while this paper studies the fee rule itself and asks which hidden bargains must be mathematically deterred.
ww: The result works because coalition size is not automatically the same thing as coalition power. A larger group has more participants, but the profitable change still has to pass through the same public mechanism: bids are submitted, transactions are selected, fees are charged, and the miner's payoff is determined. If a larger coalition can improve its position, the proof shows that the essential pressure can be isolated inside a miner-plus-two-user interaction. Two users are enough to express the conflict that one user cannot always express: one user may gain from favored treatment while another user's presence changes the allocation, payment comparison, or tie situation. Once that interaction is captured, adding more users does not create a new class of fee mechanisms under the assumptions in the abstract. Consistent tie-breaking helps because it prevents the proof from depending on arbitrary switches between equal outcomes. The intuitive lesson is that the real threshold is not many versus few; it is whether the mechanism survives the smallest coalition that can already reshuffle competition among users.
po: The payoff is a simpler target for blockchain fee-rule design. Instead of proving resistance separately for every possible number of colluding users, a designer can focus on the two-user side-contract test when c is at least two. The abstract says this collapses the class of 2-SCP mechanisms and the class of c-SCP mechanisms for any c greater than or equal to two, under consistent tie-breaking. That clarifies what must be checked and what earlier gaps mean: the important jump is from one colluding user to two, not from two to larger groups. It also gives protocol researchers a sharper way to compare proposed transaction fee mechanisms.
limits: The abstract states a formal equivalence, so the claim depends on the formal model of transaction fee mechanisms, user utility, miner utility, and side contracts used in the paper. It also depends on consistent tie-breaking; if a real protocol handles equal outcomes inconsistently, the theorem may not apply directly. The result does not say that two-user resistance is easy to achieve, only that it is sufficient for larger c within the model. It also does not prove protection against every real-world behavior around block construction, such as network delays, censorship, off-chain identity problems, or repeated long-term relationships among miners and users unless those are represented by the side-contract model.
